title: Frank's Back in Business

jokes.text: Bring in... the warthog. (snorting sounds follow)
jokes.setup: Boardroom in crisis; members debate bringing back the company's gruff founder with dramatic gravitas — 'He's a Neanderthal, an animal.'
jokes.punchline: The ominous nickname 'the warthog' is delivered with maximum dramatic weight, immediately followed by literal snorting sounds (Frank eating crow eggs).
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny cold open misdirection: the boardroom scene plays it completely straight with cinematic gravitas, then cuts to Frank literally snorting while eating crow eggs. The juxtaposition of the mythologized 'warthog' with the reality of Frank Reynolds is a perfect encapsulation of the show's ethos. The snorting sounds bridging the two scenes is elegant structural comedy.

dialogue.line: Bring in... the warthog.

jokes.text: Frank snorting while eating crow eggs in a filthy alley immediately after the dramatic 'bring in the warthog' reveal.
jokes.setup: The boardroom has just gravely announced they need their legendary founder — the 'warthog' — to save the company.
jokes.punchline: Cut to Frank literally snorting like a pig while hunched over crow eggs in an alley with Charlie, confirming the nickname is entirely apt and the legend is completely unearned.
jokes.explanation: This is the best structural joke in the cold open — a pure visual payoff to a verbal setup. The comedic gap between the mythologized 'warthog' and the reality of Frank snorting over stolen bird eggs is enormous. The snorting is diegetically motivated (his nickname) while also being literally what he's doing. Only Frank Reynolds exists at the intersection of 'legendary businessman' and 'forages for crow eggs.' Scores high on character integration and economy because zero words are needed — the image does all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Hey, Frank, how do you know that these are crow's eggs?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Because I saw a crow.

jokes.text: FRANK: Because I saw a crow.
jokes.setup: Charlie asks how Frank knows these are crow's eggs, implying some expertise or knowledge.
jokes.punchline: Frank's reasoning is comically primitive — he saw a crow, so the eggs must be crow eggs. Delivered with complete confidence.
jokes.explanation: Four words doing maximum work. Frank's total confidence in a completely idiotic logical leap is perfectly in character. The economy is exceptional — no embellishment needed. Sets up the crow egg running gag that pays off spectacularly at the end.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, boom, 24 hours is up. The found wallet is ours. Let's pop this bad boy open and see what we've won. Mr. Brian LeFeve from Quebec, you lose.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, there's a whole untapped world of bird eggs that we're not even taking advantage of.
jokes.setup: Frank and Charlie are in what appears to be a natural setting eating crow eggs as a survival/scavenging activity.
jokes.punchline: Charlie treats the discovery of bird eggs as a legitimate untapped market opportunity, applying entrepreneurial enthusiasm to something completely feral.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures Charlie's child-like enthusiasm and lack of filter. The joke works because it's completely sincere — Charlie genuinely believes this. Also plants the crow egg seed that becomes Fight Milk, making it a structural cornerstone.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, shit. Is that Canadian? Ah, throw it in the trash.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm not gonna throw it in the trash. Might be worth more than ours.

jokes.text: SWEET DEE: Is that Canadian? Ah, throw it in the trash.
jokes.setup: They open the wallet and find Canadian currency, hoping for American money.
jokes.punchline: Sweet Dee's immediate, casual dismissal of an entire country's currency as trash-worthy, with no hesitation.
jokes.explanation: Quick, mean-spirited dismissal that works through its casual confidence. The economy is good — the joke lands fast. It's a bit of a cliché (Canadian money joke) but Dee's delivery makes it sharper than it has any right to be.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Charlie can't read. He'll adapt. He'll adapt to reading?

jokes.text: Always check your breath. Right. (panting) And when you shake their hands, make sure your hands are bone dry. Dry hands. Never wet and clammy.
jokes.setup: Dennis is briefing Mac and Dee before they impersonate LeFeve's business contacts.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's elaborate coaching tips — checking breath, dry hands — are weirdly specific power-move advice delivered with the intensity of a sports coach, revealing his pathological obsession with control and presentation.
jokes.explanation: Works as character comedy — this is exactly how Dennis operates. The specificity of 'bone dry, never wet and clammy' is a nice touch. Mac's parroting 'Dry hands' shows he's absorbing this absurd wisdom uncritically.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What are you gonna do if he comes looking for it?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Uh, tell him to suck a boner.

jokes.text: Frank's taking me under his wing; He's gonna teach me how to swim with the sharks. / Charlie can't read. / He'll adapt. / He'll adapt to reading?
jokes.setup: Charlie announces Frank is mentoring him in business. Someone notes Charlie can't read.
jokes.punchline: Frank dismisses the reading problem with 'He'll adapt,' and when pushed, doubles down — implying Charlie will adapt to reading rather than finding another solution, which is both confident and completely delusional.
jokes.explanation: Multi-layered joke that uses Charlie's established illiteracy as a character trait and plays it straight. The beat where someone clarifies 'He'll adapt to reading?' is well-constructed — the follow-up question exposes the absurdity of Frank's confidence without deflating it. Perfect character integration for both Frank (oblivious optimism) and Charlie (cheerfully accepting his own limitation).

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Free shit, free shit. Jesus Christ. Act like you belong here.

jokes.text: What are you gonna do if he comes looking for it? / Uh, tell him to suck a boner. / Exactly.
jokes.setup: Mac raises the legitimate concern that the wallet's owner might come looking for it.
jokes.punchline: Sweet Dee's plan is simply 'tell him to suck a boner,' and Dennis endorses this as a legitimate strategy with 'Exactly.'
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the structure: a reasonable question gets an unreasonable answer, and the most uptight character validates it completely. 'Exactly' as a one-word punchline is perfect economy. 'Suck a boner' is crude but specific enough to feel like authentic Sunny dialogue rather than generic vulgarity.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: All right, I'll run the op. This the only entrance and/or exit, therefore if somebody comes in, I will spring off the balcony to safety.

jokes.text: ALL: Boom, I got your wallet. Boom, I got your credit cards. Boom, I got your Phillies tickets.
jokes.setup: Dennis's earlier solo 'Boom' boasting is now a group chant.
jokes.punchline: The gang has organically adopted Dennis's self-congratulatory 'boom' ritual as a collective cheer, showing how the group absorbs each other's worst impulses.
jokes.explanation: Decent callback that escalates the earlier solo moment into a group ritual. Not exceptional but shows the writers are tracking the episode's internal rhythms.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Dennis, if I had a gun with me, I'd be spraying bullets into the air as I fell.

jokes.text: Oh, fine dining and baseball food. / There's more. / Hey! Oh! Free batteries! / Hey, hey, hey, hey, hey. Calm down, calm down. / What's in here? / Free shit, free shit. / Look at all these coasters. / Jesus Christ.
jokes.setup: The gang enters a luxury stadium box suite for the first time.
jokes.punchline: Their reactions escalate from wonder at fine dining to losing their minds over free batteries and coasters, revealing that despite their pretensions, they're easily impressed by trivial free items.
jokes.explanation: The escalating frenzy is well-constructed: starts with legitimate excitement (fine dining), then goes completely unhinged over batteries and coasters. The gap between their pretensions (they're posing as wealthy business contacts) and their actual behavior (grabbing free batteries like raccoons) is the core of Sunny's comedic engine. 'Jesus Christ' as Dennis's straight-man reaction grounds the chaos perfectly.

dialogue.line: Oh, uh, yeah, yeah, hi... It's nice to finally put a face to the name.

jokes.text: Act like you belong here.
jokes.setup: Mac has just been shrieking about free batteries while they're supposed to be impersonating wealthy business associates.
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers this advice immediately after the chaos, completely unaware of how hypocritical it is given that none of them belong here either.
jokes.explanation: Four-word line that works through pure irony — Dennis is the least qualified person to give this advice given the situation. His complete lack of self-awareness is the joke. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Vic Vinegar, bodyguard. I don't shake, so don't even try.

jokes.text: This is the only entrance and/or exit, therefore if somebody comes in, I will spring off the balcony to safety. / No, no, no, no. That's a 50-foot drop. / Yes, of course, and I'm a professional, so I will tuck and roll.
jokes.setup: Dennis asks for a real exit strategy in case they get caught.
jokes.punchline: Mac's plan is to leap off a 50-foot balcony and 'tuck and roll,' which he presents as a professional maneuver.
jokes.explanation: Classic Mac joke — his delusion about his own physical capabilities is a recurring character trait. 'I'm a professional' applied to jumping off a stadium balcony is perfectly Mac. The escalation to bullets follows logically from his action-hero self-image.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Also, there are too many minorities and women working here. What's up with that?

jokes.text: Dennis, if I had a gun with me, I'd be spraying bullets into the air as I fell.
jokes.setup: Dennis dismisses the tuck-and-roll plan as insane.
jokes.punchline: Mac doesn't defend the plan — he just regrets he doesn't have a gun to make his imagined 50-foot death-leap even more cinematic.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. Mac doesn't argue against the criticism of his plan — he simply escalates it into an action-movie fantasy. The specificity of 'spraying bullets into the air as I fell' is what makes it exceptional: it's not just 'I wish I had a gun,' it's a fully realized cinematic vision of his own death-defying heroism. This is pure Mac — his self-image as an action hero colliding with objective reality. Highly quotable and perfectly constructed. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor example in terms of character specificity and surprise.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Let me ask you a question. Did I just do your job for you?

dialogue.speaker: Employee
dialogue.line: Uh, I-I guess so.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You're fired.

jokes.text: Now, from our conversations, I would have pegged you for Bill. Crazy? / Oh, yeah, we get that sometimes.
jokes.setup: Dennis (posing as LeFeve) meets Andrew Kane and Bill Larkin. He confidently declares he'd have pegged Andrew for Bill.
jokes.punchline: Bill confirms they 'get that sometimes,' validating Dennis's completely meaningless observation and creating a moment of absurd mutual delusion.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's con-man social engineering on display — he makes a meaningless observation with total confidence, and the marks validate it. Works as a quick character beat showing Dennis's manipulative charm.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I seen better-looking moose turds in Rick Moranis' backyard, ya hosers.

jokes.text: Vic Vinegar, bodyguard. I don't shake, so don't even try.
jokes.setup: Mac needs to introduce himself when asked who he is while they're impersonating LeFeve's entourage.
jokes.punchline: Mac invents an absurd alias ('Vic Vinegar') and immediately establishes a ridiculous personal rule about handshaking delivered as a tough-guy affectation.
jokes.explanation: 'Vic Vinegar' is a great comedy name — sounds fake in exactly the right way. 'I don't shake, so don't even try' is an absurd power move that only someone as deluded about their own toughness as Mac would deploy unprompted. High quotability; this is the kind of line fans repeat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: This is about the thrill of wearing another man's skin. Feeling his innermost wants and desires and being in control of his every single move.

jokes.text: Yeah, I mean, he's really more of a driver. He drives us around. / I protect their bodies. / He protects the car.
jokes.setup: Dennis quietly undercuts Mac's 'bodyguard' claim by explaining he's just a driver.
jokes.punchline: Mac insists he 'protects their bodies,' Dennis counters with 'He protects the car' — a perfect deflation that also reveals the car matters more to Dennis than Mac.
jokes.explanation: Clean three-part exchange with a satisfying structure. Dennis's 'He protects the car' is the punchline — it both demeans Mac and reveals something about Dennis's priorities. The overlapping claims create a natural comedic rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That's how you get off. Now don't you guys want to get off with me?

jokes.text: Vic, you're working. (laughs): You're working. You are. A bodyguard, you got to drive, too, stupid.
jokes.setup: Mac (as 'Vic Vinegar') tries to get a beer when Dennis orders a round.
jokes.punchline: Dennis laughs at Mac for trying to drink while 'working,' reinforcing the in-joke fiction while also genuinely humiliating Mac in front of their marks.
jokes.explanation: Decent beat that extends the bodyguard joke. Dennis's laugh is cruel in a way that's character-consistent. 'You got to drive, too, stupid' is an effective tag but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Charlie, Charlie, Charlie, we don't build anything. Leave that to the Chinks.

jokes.text: Also, there are too many minorities and women working here. What's up with that?
jokes.setup: Frank is issuing rapid-fire business directives to Charlie as if running a legitimate company turnaround.
jokes.punchline: Among legitimate-sounding instructions, Frank casually inserts a racist/sexist complaint as if it's just another agenda item, delivered with zero self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: The joke is Frank's complete lack of self-awareness — he lists this alongside 'call the press' as a routine business concern. The casualness is what makes it land as dark comedy rather than just an offensive statement. It's the character (a 1980s businessman restored to power) saying something that reveals exactly who he is.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: No, I want to eat sushi off of some Jap broad's tits.

jokes.text: The paper jam scene: Frank fixes the printer, fires the employee whose job he just did for them.
jokes.setup: An employee struggles with a jammed printer. Frank steps in with surprising competence and fixes it.
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately uses his help as grounds to fire the employee ('Did I just do your job for you?'), turning a moment of kindness into a power play.
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy construction. The setup misdirects toward Frank being unexpectedly decent, then the punchline inverts it completely — his 'help' was actually a trap. 'Did I just do your job for you?' repeated twice before firing the person is a great comic rhythm. The growling before 'You're fired' adds a perfect physical punctuation. This is the show at its darkest-funniest.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Um, bodyguards. What about bodyguards? Training bodyguards, putting them in a facility and... What about them? Oh, what about a resort?

jokes.text: If we're gonna turn this company around, we got to start cutting the crust off this shit sandwich.
jokes.setup: Frank has just fired someone and is rallying the office.
jokes.punchline: Frank's motivational business metaphor — 'cutting the crust off this shit sandwich' — is simultaneously gross, vivid, and strangely coherent as a business philosophy.
jokes.explanation: A great Frank line — it sounds almost like a real business aphorism until the 'shit sandwich' lands. The specificity (cutting the crust, not just the sandwich) adds an unexpected layer. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Masseuse
dialogue.line: I was told there'd just be one, but I can take both of you. Might get a little sore, but I'll manage.

jokes.text: Sweet Dee does a Canadian accent: 'I tell you what, I seen better-looking moose turds in Rick Moranis' backyard, ya hosers.'
jokes.setup: Dee has been trying to participate in the business meeting but is being sidelined. She decides to contribute by speaking in an exaggerated Canadian accent.
jokes.punchline: The accent is cartoonishly bad, the content is incomprehensible as a business response, and her specific reference to 'Rick Moranis' backyard' is the kind of absurdly specific detail that only Dee would choose.
jokes.explanation: The Rick Moranis name-drop is the key — it's not random, it's specifically Canadian-celebrity specific in a way that's both too obscure and too specific for anyone actually Canadian to say. Dee trying to pass as Canadian by invoking Ghostbusters trivia is peak Dee incompetence.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That's your goddamn problem, pal, you don't know your limits 'cause you're not willing to push yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I know my limits! This is my limit.

jokes.text: She's got a sense of humor that would just... You know, it gets frustrating.
jokes.setup: Dee has just said something completely unhinged in a fake Canadian accent to their business contacts.
jokes.punchline: Dennis covers by laughing off the insanity as Prudence LeFeve's 'sense of humor,' then admits to her partner that it 'gets frustrating' — a perfect understated reaction to genuine chaos.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's social-con artistry on display — he can spin anything into a plausible explanation. 'It gets frustrating' as an admission is a great quick beat. Works well but isn't exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Brian LeFeve. Who? Brian LeFeve.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: The wallet they found?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Holy shit!

jokes.text: This is about the thrill of wearing another man's skin. Feeling his innermost wants and desires and being in control of his every single move.
jokes.setup: Dennis is explaining to Mac and Dee why he wants to continue the LeFeve impersonation, framing it as a business strategy.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's explanation veers from business rationale into something that sounds unmistakably like serial killer psychology — 'wearing another man's skin' is not a normal way to describe identity roleplay.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a cornerstone of Dennis's character mythology. The language escalates from almost-plausible ('wearing another man's skin') to undeniably disturbing ('feeling his innermost wants and desires'). What makes it exceptional is that Dennis is completely sincere — there's no wink, no awareness that this is aberrant. This is the show using Dennis's established psychological profile to generate comedy that's funny precisely because of how dark it is. The 'D.E.N.N.I.S. System' universe is in full flower here. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in terms of character specificity and surprise, but adds a darker edge that elevates it slightly.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What are you talking broken English for? I thought they could understand me better if I...

jokes.text: That's how you get off. / ...Now don't you guys want to get off with me?
jokes.setup: Dennis has been describing his desire to fully inhabit LeFeve's identity and 'get off' on the thrill of control — using 'get off' in a psychological/power sense.
jokes.punchline: The phrase 'get off' reads unmistakably as sexual, and Dennis's invitation for the group to 'get off with me' creates an inadvertent (or possibly deliberate) double entendre that disturbs Mac and Dee.
jokes.explanation: The 'get off' running gag begins here and pays off magnificently at the episode's climax. What makes it work is the ambiguity: Dennis might genuinely mean psychological thrill, or he might mean something more. Mac's 'I don't know. / What?' reaction beat is crucial — it shows even Mac, who worships Dennis, is unsettled. The setup for the later payoff is excellent structural writing.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You bring us a great honor to join with us, and we have many a naked woman and the fish of pleasure for you...

jokes.text: I don't know. What? / I want you to get off with me. / Okay, okay. / Just follow my lead, guys, we're gonna get off together.
jokes.setup: Mac hesitates at Dennis's invitation to 'get off together.'
jokes.punchline: Dennis doubles down — 'Guys, we're gonna get off together' — making it progressively more uncomfortable, with Mac and Dee's reluctant compliance making it funnier.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the 'get off' joke in rapid succession is well-paced. Each repetition adds another layer of discomfort. 'Guys, we're gonna get off together' is the best version — the casual group-activity framing of what sounds like a proposition.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: There's been an abundance of crow eggs all around Philly. And crows seem to be getting bigger. By the year and the day, even.

jokes.text: What does Atwater make? / What do you mean, like, how much money does the company make? / Oh, no, I mean what do we make? / I don't follow. / We make money. / No, I know we make money. I mean, what do we build, what do we design?
jokes.setup: Charlie genuinely asks what the company actually produces, not understanding the abstraction of a holding company.
jokes.punchline: Frank keeps interpreting the question as being about profit, unable to comprehend that Charlie is asking what they actually make/build — because they don't make anything, and Frank has never thought about it that way.
jokes.explanation: This exchange works on multiple levels: Charlie's question is both naive and philosophically sharp (what does a pure financial holding company actually create?), while Frank's inability to understand the question reveals he's never examined his own business. The circular dialogue is well-constructed — each of Charlie's clarifications should make it clearer, but Frank keeps deflecting back to money. This sets up the episode's thematic point while being genuinely funny.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You're fired... You keep talking about products and quality and making things... You're out.

jokes.text: Charlie, Charlie, charlie, we don't build anything. Leave that to the Chinks.
jokes.setup: Charlie has pressed Frank on what the company actually creates or builds.
jokes.punchline: Frank's answer to 'what do we make?' is effectively 'nothing, that's for the Chinks' — both racist and a devastating critique of outsourcing-era capitalism, delivered as simple common sense.
jokes.explanation: Frank's slur is the character (a relic of a previous era) speaking in his natural register. The joke is that he's actually summarizing a real critique of American business — total offshoring — but through the lens of someone with no moral compass. Character-specific, dark, and has a satirical edge.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Fight Milk! The first alcoholic, dairy-based protein drink for bodyguards... By bodyguards!

jokes.text: Speaking of which, I want this sushi dinner to be the tits. / Oh, okay, so you want it to be, like, really expensive. / No, I want to eat sushi off of some Jap broad's tits.
jokes.setup: Frank says he wants the sushi dinner to be 'the tits,' which Charlie interprets as an intensifier meaning 'great/expensive.'
jokes.punchline: Frank clarifies that 'the tits' was not an intensifier — he literally wants to eat sushi off a woman's body. The misdirection on 'the tits' is the structural engine.
jokes.explanation: Excellent setup/punchline with a genuine misdirect. The phrase 'the tits' works naturally as an intensifier, so Charlie's interpretation is completely reasonable. Frank's clarification recontextualizes the phrase and reveals his actual (deeply gross) intent. The structure is tight: setup, reasonable misinterpretation, devastating clarification. Charlie's sincere attempt to translate Frank's request into something normal makes the punchline land harder. One of the episode's tightest joke constructions.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I drink it every morning so I can fight like the crow.

jokes.text: Hmm. (beat of silence as Charlie processes the sushi-off-tits request)
jokes.setup: Frank has just explained he wants to eat sushi off a woman's body.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's 'Hmm' and the beat of silence is his only response — not shocked, not outraged, just... processing it as if it were a logistical concern.
jokes.explanation: The 'Hmm' is doing enormous work. Charlie's total lack of moral objection — his only response is a thoughtful pause, as if working out the logistics — is both a character joke and a commentary on how normalized Frank's behavior is in Charlie's world. Perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Well, that's not Brian LeFeve! This is Brian LeFeve.

jokes.text: I am gonna get you off in ways you never believed existed.
jokes.setup: Dennis is convincing Mac and Dee to follow his lead in the impersonation scheme.
jokes.punchline: The 'get off' language continues, now with Dennis promising to 'get you off in ways you never believed existed' — clearly sexual in phrasing but ostensibly about the thrill of the con.
jokes.explanation: The 'get off' running gag continues building. 'In ways you never believed existed' escalates the already-uncomfortable language. The gag is working as a slow burn that will pay off at the episode's climax.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: This guy here... He's like, 'Dude, get a fingerprint.' And I heard, 'Get a fingertip.' And I chopped his finger off really quick

jokes.text: Oh, you got ideas? Pitch me one of your ideas right now. / Right now? Off the top of my head? / Yeah. / Um, bodyguards. / What about bodyguards? / Training bodyguards, putting them in a facility and... / What about them? / Oh, what about a resort? / That's a totally different thing. / Are you saying that because we're in a resort?
jokes.setup: Mac insists he has good business ideas and Dennis challenges him to pitch one on the spot.
jokes.punchline: Mac's idea instantly falls apart — he starts with 'bodyguards,' pivots to a 'resort,' and when Dennis points out that's a completely different concept, Mac reveals the resort idea came from their current location.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant exchange that reveals Mac's total intellectual bankruptcy in real time. The pivot from 'bodyguards' to 'a resort' is funny on its own, but 'Are you saying that because we're in a resort?' is the perfect punchline — it confirms Mac's ideas are entirely reactive to his immediate surroundings, not actual thought. The dialogue rhythm is excellent, with Dennis's one-word questions ('What about them?') forcing Mac to expose his emptiness.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Just a couple of people who totally got off, bro.

jokes.text: Oh, hey, you must be Mr. LeFeve? / Uh, yeah, that's me. / Surprise. I'm all yours. I was told there'd just be one, but I can take both of you. Might get a little sore, but I'll manage.
jokes.setup: Dennis has arranged a 'surprise' for LeFeve in the locker room, knowing LeFeve is apparently 'into' something specific.
jokes.punchline: The masseuse/masseur arrives and their completely innocent massage-industry language ('I can take both of you, might get a little sore') sounds unmistakably sexual given the setup about LeFeve's specific tastes.
jokes.explanation: The misdirection works because both interpretations are possible simultaneously. 'Might get a little sore, but I'll manage' in a massage context is completely innocent but reads as the opposite given the setup. The joke is in the audience's mind as much as the dialogue.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Just a couple of people who totally got off, bro.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You did?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Mm-hmm, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Big time, yeah.

jokes.text: LeFeve's into banging little Asian boys, so we're done, right? / If we're gonna do this thing, we need to see things through. / Dennis, are you gonna have sex with a tiny Asian boy? / I'm gonna see how far I can go.
jokes.setup: Mac has figured out that the masseuse is not what he thought and that Dennis's plan is about to cross a serious line.
jokes.punchline: Mac asks point-blank if Dennis is going to have sex with a child; Dennis responds not with denial but with 'I'm gonna see how far I can go' — which reveals that for Dennis, the line is not a moral question but a personal challenge.
jokes.explanation: One of the darkest jokes in the episode and one of the best. 'I'm gonna see how far I can go' as Dennis's response to whether he'll commit a serious crime is not a punchline that arrives with a laugh track — it's the kind of line that makes the audience gasp and then laugh. It's perfectly in character (Dennis treats everything as a personal challenge and limit-testing exercise) while being genuinely disturbing. The specificity of 'tiny Asian boy' makes it funnier and more horrible simultaneously, which is precisely the register Always Sunny operates in.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Some women just don't know how.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I don't know what it is. Sometimes it's only the guy who gets off.

jokes.text: That's your goddamn problem, pal, you don't know your limits 'cause you're not willing to push yourself. / I know my limits! This is my limit. I quit. / You quit? / Yes! / Well, guess what, pal, you can't quit 'cause you're fired, Vic! You're out of here!
jokes.setup: Mac refuses to participate further in Dennis's escalating scheme and quits.
jokes.punchline: Dennis fires Mac from his fake job (bodyguard for someone he's pretending to be) rather than accept Mac's resignation — a completely meaningless power move in an entirely fictional hierarchy.
jokes.explanation: Dennis insisting he has the power to fire Mac from a fake job, using a fake name, in a fake identity — purely to have the last word — is perfect Dennis. 'You can't quit 'cause you're fired, Vic!' is quotable precisely because of the absurdity of the power dynamics. The callback to 'Vic Vinegar' by name is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Some women just don't know how.

jokes.text: Oh, only the one set of clubs? / Yeah, you're a caddy. / Clubs... this is a golf... Good. Yeah, okay. Well, that's better than what I was about to...
jokes.setup: After the locker room incident, Mac has been given a new role in the scheme. He sees only one set of clubs.
jokes.punchline: He's just a caddy — an enormous relief compared to what he was apparently just asked to do. 'That's better than what I was about to...' trails off, confirming the audience's suspicion about what happened in the locker room.
jokes.explanation: The trailing 'that's better than what I was about to...' does the work of a callback without spelling it out — the audience fills in the gap, which is funnier than explicit confirmation. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I stripped the company, sold it to the Chinks, and they shut it down. In a sense, you're all fired.

jokes.text: I need to switch gears. I almost... Yeah. / Take your time.
jokes.setup: Mac is clearly shaken from whatever happened in the locker room.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's 'Take your time' is said with the patience of a golf instructor, completely ignoring that his friend just had to 'switch gears' from something traumatic. The silence and Mac needing a moment is the visual/implied comedy.
jokes.explanation: A quiet beat that extends the locker room callback. Dennis's breezy 'Take your time' while Mac processes something disturbing is good character work. Not a big laugh but adds texture.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I stripped the company, sold it to the Chinks, and they shut it down. In a sense, you're all fired.

jokes.text: Mac's visible gear-shift after almost doing something terrible in the locker room — 'I need to switch gears. I almost... Yeah.' / 'Take your time.'
jokes.setup: Mac arrives at the golf course having just escaped the locker room situation.
jokes.punchline: His obvious trauma — 'I almost... yeah' — combined with Dennis's breezy 'take your time' (implying he has no idea what Mac went through) is a reaction beat that lets the audience fill in what almost happened.
jokes.explanation: What the audience imagines is funnier than anything explicit. 'I almost... yeah' and 'take your time' do tremendous work. This is excellent economy — the unspoken thing is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I thought you loved the company.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I do. But not more than money.

jokes.text: Okay, first off, your dry cleaning's all done, the company jet's been upgraded. I got rid of that piece of trash.
jokes.setup: Charlie is reporting business accomplishments to Frank, trying to prove his worth as an advisor.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's business accomplishments are entirely logistical/personal services rather than anything substantive — dry cleaning, jet upgrade. 'Got rid of that piece of trash' refers to the previous jet, delivered with surprising savagery.
jokes.explanation: Decent beat showing Charlie adapting to the role of corporate fixer in the most literal possible way. Not exceptional but functional — it sets up the more important revelation about LeFeve.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I do. But not more than money.

jokes.text: Brian LeFeve. / Who? / Brian LeFeve. / The wallet they found? / Holy shit! / Yeah. / He was probably there to see me.
jokes.setup: Charlie has discovered the controlling shareholder of Atwater is Brian LeFeve — the name on the wallet the gang found.
jokes.punchline: Frank's instant conclusion — 'He was probably there to see me' — reveals his enormous ego as the most natural explanation for a coincidence.
jokes.explanation: Good plot-comedy intersection. Frank's ego-driven leap to 'he was there to see me' is perfectly in character and also happens to be correct, which is funnier than if he'd been wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Speaking of which, tell me more about this Crowtein.

jokes.text: Charlie attempting a Japanese accent: 'Ah, welcome, welcome. You bring us a great honor to join with us, and we have many a naked woman and the fish of pleasure for you...'
jokes.setup: Frank is meeting with the Japanese businessman Nakashori. Charlie decides to help by speaking in a broken Japanese accent to make communication easier.
jokes.punchline: The accent is offensive, the content is bizarre ('fish of pleasure'), and Charlie genuinely believes this is helping. His logic — speaking 'broken English' so they understand him better — is completely backwards.
jokes.explanation: 'Fish of pleasure' is a genuinely funny invention. Charlie's earnest belief that speaking badly will help a Japanese person understand English better is exactly the kind of confident stupidity that defines the character. The parallel to Dee's Canadian accent is implicit — both characters resort to terrible accents as their social strategy.

jokes.text: A few interesting facts about our city. Uh, there's been an abundance of crow eggs all around Philly. And crows seem to be getting bigger. By the year and the day, even. And their eggs, of course, are getting bigger as well. Perhaps our companies, with this information, could find a way to create some products off these new...
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to contribute to a business meeting with Nakashori. He has been repeatedly told to focus on real business matters.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's business pitch to a Japanese corporation involves the growing size of Philadelphia crows and their eggs, which he genuinely believes is actionable market intelligence.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant callback that also sets up the Fight Milk payoff. Charlie's crow egg obsession from the opening has now infiltrated a formal business meeting as his best idea. 'By the year and the day, even' is a perfect Charlie-ism — not 'by the year,' not 'by the day,' but both, delivered with authority about data he has absolutely made up. The specificity of crow egg market intelligence as a corporate pitch is perfectly absurd. High character integration: only Charlie would do this.

jokes.text: You're fired. / What? / Because you're not getting it. It's not sinkin' in. / I don't get it? / No. / Where did you get that awesome insider info from, about Brian LeFeve? / That was pretty big. / Well, that was good, Charlie.
jokes.setup: Frank fires Charlie for being incompetent, then immediately compliments him on the LeFeve intel.
jokes.punchline: Frank fires Charlie and within the same breath begins praising his work, apparently unaware of or unconcerned with the contradiction — he just fired him for not 'getting it' but Charlie clearly got something right.
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank management style — fire first, praise immediately after, with no awareness of the contradiction. Charlie's bewilderment ('I don't get it? / No') is well-played. Good character beat.

jokes.text: Well, thanks for the insider info, Mac, but that did not work. Frank canned me. / He did? Yeah! What a dick!
jokes.setup: Charlie reports that Frank fired him despite the good intel.
jokes.punchline: Mac's instant 'What a dick!' — as if Frank firing Charlie for being incompetent in a business meeting is a personal outrage rather than a reasonable reaction.
jokes.explanation: Quick transitional joke. 'What a dick!' is a reliable laugh but not exceptional. The scene functions more as plot than comedy at this point.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie bond with LeFeve over shared business philosophy: 'It's all about the product for me.' / 'That's what I was saying to Frank the entire time.' / 'Money has nothing to do with it.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie, having been rejected by Dennis and Frank respectively, commiserate with the actual Brian LeFeve (who they don't recognize).
jokes.punchline: They bond enthusiastically over business philosophy with the very man whose identity is being stolen — and their shared philosophy is sincere but also hilariously naive given the context.
jokes.explanation: Great structural irony — Mac and Charlie are unknowingly networking with the man whose wallet and identity they stole. The sincerity of their business philosophy conversation (Charlie genuinely cares about products) makes the dramatic irony funnier. 'Money has nothing to do with it' is a great line from the gang member who stole a wallet to attend a baseball game.

jokes.text: Does the name Brian LeFeve mean anything to you guys? (indistinct talking)
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie have been enthusiastically bonding with the real LeFeve without recognizing him.
jokes.punchline: LeFeve asks if his own name means anything to them — it means everything, it's literally the name on the wallet they stole — and the audience knows before Mac and Charlie process it.
jokes.explanation: Good beat of dramatic irony where the audience is ahead of the characters. The '(indistinct talking)' implies Mac and Charlie's scrambling reaction, which is implied comedy. The reveal is well-timed.

jokes.text: Okay, LeFeve, enough. We took you out the yacht, we took you to the zoo, we took you to that massage parlor and paid to have them jerk you both off.
jokes.setup: The Wheeler Group is frustrated by Dennis's stalling. They're recounting everything they've done to court LeFeve.
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from normal corporate entertaining (yacht, zoo) to 'paid to have them jerk you both off' — an activity that's both definitively sexual and delivered with the same casual matter-of-factness as the zoo visit.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'yacht' to 'zoo' to 'jerk you both off' is a perfect three-part list joke where the third item departs wildly from the pattern. The casualness of delivery — as if paid sexual services are standard corporate entertaining — is the register that makes it work in the context of this episode's themes.

jokes.text: Not so fast! There's something you all need to know about Atwater! (laughing crazily) Prepare to have your minds blown. We got a video.
jokes.setup: Frank is about to address the shareholders meeting with real business information.
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie burst in to hijack the meeting with what appears to be a business pitch, presented with manic energy wildly disproportionate to the context.
jokes.explanation: The setup for the Fight Milk video — works as escalation toward the payoff rather than a standalone joke. 'Prepare to have your minds blown. We got a video.' is a good beat.

jokes.text: Fight Milk! The first alcoholic, dairy-based protein drink for bodyguards... By bodyguard! I drink it every morning so I can fight like the crow.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie present their business idea via video at a shareholders meeting.
jokes.punchline: Fight Milk — an 'alcoholic, dairy-based protein drink for bodyguards, by bodyguards' — is the logical endpoint of crow eggs + Mac's bodyguard delusion. The slogan 'fight like the crow' is the crown jewel.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and a classic Always Sunny moment. Fight Milk is the perfect synthesis of two separate episode threads: Charlie's crow egg obsession and Mac's bodyguard delusion. The product concept itself is absurdist (why would bodyguards need alcohol AND protein?), but the specificity — 'by bodyguards, for bodyguards' — gives it the structure of a real marketing pitch. 'Fight like the crow' as a tagline is genuinely inspired: it's catchy, it makes no sense as a fitness aspiration, and it's completely sincere. This is a cultural touchstone for Always Sunny fans — it became real merchandise. The double callback (crow eggs + bodyguard identity) makes it earn its impact rather than arriving from nowhere.

jokes.text: I drink it every morning so I can fight like the crow. (bird cawing) Just get out of the way. There we go. It's all about the product shot.
jokes.setup: During the Fight Milk video, there's apparently a live crow or crow sound effect being used for production value.
jokes.punchline: The behind-the-scenes chaos of a crow getting in the way of their product shot bleeds into the video — they're apparently shooting this with a live crow, and it's not cooperating. 'Just get out of the way. There we go.' reveals this is a barely-produced commercial.
jokes.explanation: The production value of the Fight Milk video collapsing in real time is excellent visual comedy. The fact that they apparently wrangled an actual crow for their commercial — and the crow is uncooperative — adds a layer of deranged commitment to the bit.

jokes.text: Crow's egg! (bird cawing) Milk! (bird cawing) Made fresh. By bodyguards. And Charlie.
jokes.setup: The Fight Milk commercial lists its ingredients dramatically.
jokes.punchline: 'And Charlie' — Charlie is listed as an ingredient, not a co-creator, but as a component of the drink. Also: crow eggs and milk are the ingredients of an 'alcoholic, dairy-based protein drink,' which makes no chemical sense.
jokes.explanation: 'And Charlie' is a perfectly economical joke. The commercial lists the ingredients (crow's egg, milk) with equal dramatic weight, then adds 'And Charlie' — suggesting Charlie is either an ingredient or an afterthought co-brand. The ambiguity is funnier than clarity would be.

jokes.text: Watch as profits soar high as a crow. (cash register bell ringing) (bird cawing) (Mac caws) Watch your profits soar high as a crow. (Mac caws) Ow. / Sorry.
jokes.setup: The Fight Milk commercial promises financial returns using crow metaphors.
jokes.punchline: Mac is making crow sounds himself for the commercial, there's apparently a collision or physical mishap ('Ow'), and Charlie apologizes — the commercial is falling apart in real time.
jokes.explanation: Mac making crow sounds ('caws') is good physical comedy. The 'Ow. / Sorry.' suggests an on-camera physical accident that made it into the final cut — perfectly consistent with how incompetently this commercial was produced.

jokes.text: Wait, I thought we said I was gonna... Profits... Yeah, go with your right. To the right hand.
jokes.setup: The Fight Milk video is still playing; Mac and Charlie argue about positioning.
jokes.punchline: They are visibly figuring out choreography in real time within the pitch video itself — revealing the entire thing is being improvised, and their priority is getting the blocking right rather than the pitch.
jokes.explanation: Extends the 'shambolic production' joke. 'Go with your right. To the right hand.' mid-presentation is evidence of how live and unscripted this 'professional' pitch is.

jokes.text: So what's this got to do with Atwater? / Oh, nothing.
jokes.setup: The shareholders have just watched a commercial for Fight Milk presented in the middle of a corporate meeting ostensibly about their company.
jokes.punchline: When asked the obvious question — what does Fight Milk have to do with Atwater — the answer is simply 'Oh, nothing.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat joke. The question is obvious; the answer is total honesty with zero shame. 'Oh, nothing' — the casual 'Oh' preceding the admission of complete irrelevance — is a masterclass in comedic economy. This is the punchline to a 17-minute setup: they hijacked a shareholders meeting to pitch a drink that has nothing to do with the company.

jokes.text: Oh! Yeah, right. Well, that's not Brian LeFeve! (crowd murmuring) This is Brian LeFeve. (crowd gasping) Yeah. Yeah.
jokes.setup: Mac prompts Charlie about 'the news' at the shareholders meeting.
jokes.punchline: Charlie reveals that the controlling shareholder (Dennis's impersonation target) is dead — producing evidence to prove it in a room full of investors — while Mac and Charlie react with the casual energy of people sharing mild news.
jokes.explanation: The reveal lands well — 'this is Brian LeFeve' producing a morgue photo is a good dark comedy beat. The crowd gasping versus Mac and Charlie's matter-of-fact energy is the core of the joke.

jokes.text: No, um, we just didn't want to lead with the Atwater news because we figured you wouldn't stick around to watch the video.
jokes.setup: Asked why they led with the Fight Milk video instead of the actual news about Atwater.
jokes.punchline: Their reasoning is completely backwards — they buried the real news so people would watch their commercial pitch. It's simultaneously terrible PR strategy and extremely consistent with how these characters think.
jokes.explanation: The logic is completely wrong but internally consistent — they prioritized their vanity project over the meeting's actual purpose. That's exactly who these characters are.

jokes.text: That's not Brian LeFeve! / (crowd murmuring) This is Brian LeFeve. / (crowd gasping) / Yeah. / Yeah, apparently he came to the bar to talk to Frank, and I didn't recognize him from his picture in his wallet, but I did recognize it when I saw that dead face in the morgue.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie have revealed that Dennis is not the real LeFeve. They now present the real LeFeve.
jokes.punchline: LeFeve is dead. Charlie recognized him from the morgue. The 'actual business news' about Atwater is that the controlling shareholder is dead, which Charlie announces with the same energy as a product reveal.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that the real LeFeve is dead is perfectly timed and well-constructed — the 'crowd murmuring' and 'crowd gasping' reactions sold by the audience surrogates. 'I did recognize it when I saw that dead face in the morgue' is an excellent line — Charlie's matter-of-fact description of identifying a corpse in a corporate meeting is perfectly wrong-register delivery.

jokes.text: Yeah, he was having a couple drinks and then... But Charlie was in the bathroom cleaning it out. / I was working. / I'm like, 'Dude, take it out to the alley.' And then I guess he's out in the alley, he comes back in, he forgot his wallet. Mac's like, 'ID please.' / Yeah, he doesn't get in without an ID. That's just the rule.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are explaining to a boardroom how the controlling shareholder came to die.
jokes.punchline: The story reveals a chain of gang incompetence directly contributed to LeFeve's death: Charlie locked him out of the bathroom, Mac enforced a no-ID policy that left LeFeve without identification, forcing him into the alley where he was stabbed.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best sequences. The escalating story of how Mac and Charlie inadvertently caused a man's death through sheer petty rule-enforcement is dark comedy perfection. 'Yeah, he doesn't get in without an ID. That's just the rule.' delivered while explaining to a boardroom how their policy got someone killed is exactly the register of casual monstrousness that defines Always Sunny at its best. Each beat — Charlie in the bathroom, Mac's ID rule — adds another layer of complicity.

jokes.text: Why do you got his finger? / Oh. (laughing) / Well, the whole finger thing is... This was a miscommunication.
jokes.setup: In the midst of explaining LeFeve's death, it's revealed that one of them has LeFeve's severed finger.
jokes.punchline: The finger's presence is treated as a minor embarrassment — a 'miscommunication' — rather than the horrifying thing it is.
jokes.explanation: 'This was a miscommunication' as the explanation for having a dead man's severed finger at a corporate meeting is perfectly calibrated Always Sunny darkness. The casualness of the admission — the laughing, the 'oh' — treats this as a minor logistical error rather than something criminal.

jokes.text: He's like, 'Dude, get a fingerprint.' And I heard, 'Get a fingertip.' And I chopped his finger off really quick and then I'm like, 'Is this what you want?' He starts screaming, you know.
jokes.setup: Charlie explains the miscommunication that resulted in a severed finger.
jokes.punchline: The 'fingerprint' vs 'fingertip' mishearing is the structural engine. Charlie acted immediately and without hesitation ('chopped his finger off really quick'), then expressed confusion when the response was negative.
jokes.explanation: The best structurally constructed joke in the episode. 'Fingerprint' vs 'fingertip' is a genuine near-homophone mishearing that's both plausible and devastating in context. 'Chopped his finger off really quick' — the word 'really quick' is what makes it exceptional, implying Charlie's decisive action before thinking. 'Is this what you want?' as the follow-up question, delivered while presumably holding a severed finger at a morgue, is perfect comedic logic. 'He starts screaming, you know' — the casual 'you know' treats this as a universal experience. This approaches the caliber of the 'Snip snap' anchor example in terms of dark escalation and quotability. Classic Always Sunny.

jokes.text: And I'm like, 'Is this what you want?' He starts screaming, you know.
jokes.setup: Charlie has explained he chopped off a dead man's finger.
jokes.punchline: The 'Is this what you want?' — with Charlie holding up a severed finger — and the person's screaming response, treated by Charlie as an inexplicable overreaction ('you know'), is a perfect button.
jokes.explanation: The 'you know' at the end is the word that makes this. Charlie presents someone screaming at being shown a severed finger as a universally relatable reaction — 'you know' — as if screaming is the natural response Charlie expected, not a reason to question what he did. Beautifully in character.

jokes.text: If Brian LeFeve is dead... then who the hell are these people? / Just a couple of people who totally got off, bro.
jokes.setup: The shareholders realize Dennis and his associates are not who they claimed to be. Someone asks who they actually are.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's answer: they 'totally got off' — the culmination of the 'get off' running gag, now delivered as the punchline to the entire episode's Dennis plotline.
jokes.explanation: Perfect running gag payoff. The 'get off' thread has been building since Dennis's manifesto about 'wearing another man's skin,' and here it arrives as the answer to the question of who these people are. Dennis's pride in having 'totally got off' — with 'bro' adding a casual frat-boy energy — recontextualizes everything that came before while also being maximally weird and funny as a standalone answer. 'Just a couple of people who totally got off, bro' is an all-time Sunny line. The structure — a 10+ minute payoff to a running setup — is exceptional writing.

jokes.text: What? / You did? / Mm... Are you serious? / Mm-hmm, yeah. / Just... during this? / (whoops) / Big time, yeah.
jokes.setup: Shareholders are trying to understand what Dennis means by 'got off.'
jokes.punchline: Dennis's enthusiastic confirmation ('Big time, yeah') and whooping makes clear that the 'getting off' was real and ongoing throughout the entire scheme, while the shareholders' confused processing adds comedic texture.
jokes.explanation: The continuation of the payoff scene. The shareholders' genuine confusion ('Just... during this?') and Dennis's enthusiastic 'Big time, yeah' — the whooping — makes this sequence one sustained burst of comedic energy. Each confirmation escalates the absurdity.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah, I got off a couple times when we were watching the video presentation. Then when he called me out for not being Brian LeFeve? Whoo, that got me big time. That did it? Oh, man, did I get off.
jokes.setup: Dennis is itemizing the specific moments during the scheme when he 'got off.'
jokes.punchline: He got off during the Fight Milk video, then especially when publicly exposed as a fraud — the humiliation and exposure was actually the peak experience for him.
jokes.explanation: The specific itemization of when Dennis 'got off' is exceptional character work. The revelation that being publicly exposed as a fraud — 'that got me big time' — is his peak experience tells us everything about Dennis Reynolds as a character: he gets off on the drama itself, not just the control. This is both a great standalone joke and a profound (and disturbing) character statement. The 'Whoo' in the middle of the sentence is a perfect physical punctuation.

jokes.text: Yeah, and then he showed the finger. / That was the big one. / A dead finger got you off. / That was the climax, really.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are cataloguing what got Dennis off during the meeting.
jokes.punchline: The dead man's severed finger was 'the climax' for Dennis — both the sexual punchline of the running gag and the reveal that Dennis's kinks involve genuine horror.
jokes.explanation: The convergence of two running gags — the severed finger and the 'get off' thread — in the word 'climax' is structurally perfect. 'That was the climax, really' as Dennis's clinical description of his peak experience at a dead man's finger is both hilarious and deeply wrong. The shareholder's incredulous 'A dead finger got you off' as a straight-man line is excellent contrast.

jokes.text: It was mostly sexual.
jokes.setup: Someone in the room says they're confused about what 'getting off' means in this context.
jokes.punchline: Dennis clarifies: 'It was mostly sexual.' — The 'mostly' is the word that destroys the ambiguity that had sustained the gag, while also suggesting it was partially something else.
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfect economy, maximum impact. 'It was mostly sexual' is the best button to the 'get off' gag possible because: (1) 'mostly' acknowledges the dual meaning without resolving it cleanly; (2) it confirms what we suspected while leaving the 'not entirely sexual' part mysterious; (3) it's the kind of clarification that makes everything worse; (4) the deadpan delivery in a corporate boardroom is the ultimate Dennis move. This is anchor-level economy — three words that couldn't be replaced with anything better. Perfectly quotable, deserves a 10 for quotability.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, it was amazing. / It was mostly sexual.
jokes.setup: Dennis is wrapping up his account of the experience.
jokes.punchline: 'It was mostly sexual' — the qualifier 'mostly' is the punchline. Not 'it was sexual,' but 'mostly' — implying that some non-sexual portion of the experience was something else entirely, which is somehow more disturbing.
jokes.explanation: Four words that may be the best joke in the episode. 'Mostly sexual' as a clarification — not a full admission, but a partial one with an implied remainder — is exactly the right level of specificity to be both a punchline and a character revelation. The word 'mostly' does enormous comedy work: it acknowledges the sexual component while suggesting the rest defies categorization. It's simultaneously Dennis being uncharacteristically honest AND more disturbing for the honesty. This line alone justifies the entire 'get off' setup.

jokes.text: God damn you, okay? You know what? I could've gotten some cash out of these men. I could've gotten a free pair of shoes, but no, you said, 'Hang in there, I'll help you get off, I'll help you get off, Dee.' 'I'll show you how to do it.'
jokes.setup: Dee confronts Dennis about how the scheme turned out.
jokes.punchline: Dee's complaint is not that Dennis involved her in fraud or that she's in trouble — it's that she didn't get cash or shoes. And her parroting of Dennis's 'get off' invitations recontextualizes them as explicit promises that weren't kept.
jokes.explanation: Dee's priorities — 'cash' and 'a free pair of shoes' — are perfect character work. Her repeating Dennis's 'get off' lines back at him in a frustrated tone retroactively makes all of Dennis's earlier invitations sound like broken promises.

jokes.text: And then you leave me all on my own to try and just get off all by myself without even... I did everything that I could. / I don't understand why you couldn't get off. / It's not my fault. / Some women just don't know how. / What?!
jokes.setup: Dee complains she couldn't 'get off' during the scheme. Dennis responds.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's 'Some women just don't know how' — applied to 'getting off' in the psychological con-game sense — lands as an incredibly condescending statement about women's sexuality, made more absurd by the context in which it's being said.
jokes.explanation: Dennis applying pickup-artist/sexist logic ('some women just don't know how') to what is ostensibly a discussion of a con game's psychological rewards is a perfect convergence. The double meaning fully collapses here in the most uncomfortable way. Dee's 'What?!' is the ideal reaction — she can't tell whether Dennis is being sexist about the con or about sex.

jokes.text: Well, look, I don't know what the hell's going on over there. But I can tell you something, that there is something really palpable, wonderful going on over here. I love this company. I love it more than life. I built this company with these hands.
jokes.setup: Frank interrupts the chaos to deliver a passionate speech about his love for Atwater.
jokes.punchline: Frank's heartfelt declaration of love for Atwater — 'more than life' — is immediately undercut by his phone ringing and his subsequent announcement that he's already sold and gutted the company.
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank misdirect. The speech is completely sincere in delivery, making the immediate betrayal funnier. 'I love it more than life' is a good setup for the reversal. Functions as the episode's thematic punchline about the nature of business and Frank's character.

jokes.text: All right, that's it. It's over, you can all go. The company's gone. / What are you talking about? / I stripped the company, sold it to the Chinks, and they shut it down. / In a sense, you're all fired. Out.
jokes.setup: Frank has just delivered a passionate speech about loving the company. His phone rings.
jokes.punchline: He's already sold and gutted the company during his own passionate speech about loving it. 'In a sense, you're all fired' is a masterwork of understatement — in what sense is it NOT being fired?
jokes.explanation: The episode's thematic punchline. Frank's passionate declaration of love for his company was simultaneous with him arranging its sale — the speech was either cover or just Frank being emotionally compartmentalized to a sociopathic degree. 'In a sense, you're all fired' is the best kind of understatement: it's literally what's happening, so the 'in a sense' qualifier is comic precision. The structure is perfect — the speech sets up the reversal, the phone call triggers it, and 'you're all fired' lands as both a plot event and a punchline.

jokes.text: I do. But not more than money. And I just made a shitload of it. You get it? / Yeah. / See, Charlie?
jokes.setup: Charlie (and others) are confused about how Frank could sell the company he just professed to love.
jokes.punchline: Frank's explanation: he loves the company, just not more than money. This is a simple, coherent value statement that is completely amoral — and Charlie's 'yeah' suggests he actually does get it now.
jokes.explanation: 'But not more than money' is a great line — it's simultaneously a critique of capitalism and a perfect Frank Reynolds character statement. 'You get it? / Yeah.' — Charlie's understanding is both a beat of genuine character growth (he now understands how finance works) and a depressing one (he's internalized Frank's values). The 'See, Charlie?' callback to Charlie's earlier questions about what the company makes is implicit but resonant.

jokes.text: Out. / You can all go. / Thank you, and good-bye. / Get out, get out, go.
jokes.setup: Frank has just fired everyone in the building.
jokes.punchline: Frank's shooing of the entire company — 'out,' 'get out, get out, go' — with the energy of clearing guests from a dinner party is the final expression of his complete indifference to everyone.
jokes.explanation: Frank mass-firing people with 'get out, get out, go' energy is a good button. Not exceptional as a written joke but lands well in performance.

jokes.text: Speaking of which, tell me more about this Crowtein.
jokes.setup: Frank has just explained his entire business philosophy. The scene seems to be wrapping.
jokes.punchline: Frank's final line is asking about 'Crowtein' — the Fight Milk product, now rebranded — suggesting he's genuinely interested in investing in or developing crow egg protein. The word 'Crowtein' is itself a portmanteau joke.
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing callback that ties the entire crow egg thread together from scene one. 'Crowtein' as a word is funny on its own — it's exactly the kind of branding that sounds almost plausible. Frank asking about it seriously recontextualizes his dismissal of Charlie's 'product' obsession: when there's money in crow protein, Frank's interested. This also retroactively validates Charlie's instinct from the opening. It's the ideal closer — economical, character-specific, funny as a word, and a true callback to the episode's first joke.

tmdb_overview: With Charlie under his wing, Frank cleans up so he can get his hands dirty and help out his old company with one last big merger. An unwritten rule of the bar gets the rest of the gang caught up in a case of mistaken identity.
